blocks.text: I can state when outcomes will be equally likely.
In this lesson you will look at things that can happen in a trial, list them, and decide when they have the same chance of happening.
Tap each word to see what it means.

items.def: A trial is a single predefined test.
An outcome is a result of a trial.
A sample space is all the possible outcomes of a trial. A sample space diagram is a systematic way of producing a sample space.
Likelihood describes the chance that a particular event will occur.

blocks.text: A **trial** is a single predefined test. Here are some examples of trials:
An **outcome** is just ONE result of a trial. It is not all the results.
The set of ALL the possible outcomes of a trial is called the {sample space}.
We write a sample space using set notation: curly brackets around a list of the outcomes.
ξ = ❴outcome 1, outcome 2, outcome 3, …❵

blocks.label: What is ξ?
blocks.text: ξ is the Greek letter **xi**. It is used for the universal set. In probability, it stands for the set of all the possible outcomes of a trial.
It does not matter what order you list the outcomes in.
Jacob is going to spin a spinner once. Its sectors say **win** and **lose**. What are the possible outcomes?
Step 1: The trial is one spin of the spinner.
Step 2: The spinner could land on either win or lose.
ξ = ❴win, lose❵

blocks.label: Could Jacob draw?
blocks.text: No. A draw is not one of the possible outcomes, so it is not in the sample space. You either win or you lose.

Only outcomes in the sample space are possible. A spinner with ξ = ❴A, B, C❵ cannot land on J, and one with ξ = ❴1, 2, 3, 4❵ cannot give a negative number, but it can give a cube number because 1 is a cube number.

slides.title: Watch out! Sectors are not outcomes

blocks.text: A spinner has four sectors: two say **win** and two say **lose**. Alex says there are four possible outcomes. Sofia says there are two. Who is right?

blocks.label: Tap to find out
blocks.text: Sofia is right. The only possible outcomes are win and lose. Several sectors can show the same outcome, but the sample space only lists each different outcome once: ξ = ❴win, lose❵.
Count the {different outcomes}, not the number of sectors.
Sample spaces are not only for spinners. A coin flipped once has the sample space ξ = ❴heads, tails❵. A regular six-sided dice rolled once has ξ = ❴1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6❵.
The sample space depends on how the trial is defined. Aisha, Lucas and Sam are playing a board game.

items.title: trial = a roll of the dice

blocks.text: If the trial is the game, the outcomes are the possible winners.

blocks.q: Pick the correct sample space for each trial.

items.q: Trial: a spinner with sectors red, blue, blue, green is spun once.
Trial: Ana, Ben and Cal play a board game. The trial is the whole game.
How many outcomes are in the sample space for rolling a regular six-sided dice once?

blocks.text: Jacob spins a spinner. If it lands on win he gets a prize. Look at the size of the sectors.
When the win sector and the lose sector are the same size, the spinner is as likely to land on win as on lose. So the outcomes are {equally likely}.
If one sector is bigger than the other, the outcomes are not equally likely, so the spinner does not seem fair.
{Equally likely} outcomes have the same chance, or likelihood, of happening.

slides.title: Worked example: who gets the cookie?

blocks.text: Alex and Sofia roll a regular six-sided dice for the last cookie. Sofia gets it if the dice shows a multiple of 3. Otherwise Alex gets it. So ξ = ❴Alex, Sofia❵. Is this fair?
Step 1: Multiples of 3 on the dice: 3 and 6. That is 2 numbers for Sofia.
Step 2: The other numbers: 1, 2, 4 and 5. That is 4 numbers for Alex.
Step 3: Alex has more numbers, so the outcomes are not equally likely. Alex is more likely to get the cookie.

blocks.label: A fairer rule
blocks.text: Lucas and Jun use even or odd instead. The even numbers are 2, 4, 6 and the odd numbers are 1, 3, 5. Each of them has 3 numbers, so ξ = ❴Lucas, Jun❵ has equally likely outcomes.
A regular six-sided dice is rolled once. Count the numbers for each outcome, then decide.

items.q: ξ = ❴rolling a prime number, not a prime number❵
ξ = ❴rolling more than 2, rolling 2 or less❵

blocks.text: Aisha flips a fair coin. Tails has not come up for a while, so she thinks the next flip will probably be tails. Is she right?

blocks.label: What is wrong with Aisha’s reasoning?
blocks.text: The two outcomes, heads and tails, are always equally likely. They are not affected by previous results.
A charity raffle gives each person a number from 1 to 100. One number is picked randomly from a box. Laura has number 1 and thinks she will never win, because Jun’s number is in the middle.

blocks.label: Why is Laura wrong?
blocks.text: Each number is equally likely to be picked, regardless of its size.

blocks.label: What about rolling a 6?
blocks.text: Rolling a 6 is not harder than rolling any other number. The random nature of rolling a dice means all the outcomes are equally likely.

slides.title: More than two equally likely outcomes

blocks.text: Andeep spins a spinner once. Are all the outcomes equally likely? Look at how much of the spinner each letter takes up.

items: All sectors are the same size and each letter has its own sector: equally likely.
All sectors are the same size and there are two sectors for each letter: still equally likely.
All sectors are the same size but there are fewer sectors for C than for A or B: NOT equally likely.
B has more sectors but they are smaller. Each large sector is the same size as two small sectors, so each letter still has the same amount of space: equally likely.

blocks.text: It is the {amount of space} each outcome takes up that matters, not the number of sectors.

blocks.q: Are the outcomes of each trial equally likely? Tap a trial, then tap its column.

items.text: Spinner: 5 equal sectors labelled A, B, C, D, E
Spinner: 6 equal sectors, two each of A, B and C
Spinner: 6 equal sectors, three A, two B and one C
Dice rolled: multiple of 3 or not a multiple of 3
Raffle numbers 1 to 100: number 1 or number 50 picked
Spinner: red takes up half; blue is two small sectors that together take up the other half

blocks.q: A regular six-sided dice is rolled once.

items.q: Kim moves on a 1 or 2, Lee on a 3 or 4, Max on a 5 or 6. Are Kim, Lee and Max equally likely to move?
Kim moves on a 1, Lee on a 2 or 3, Max on a 4, 5 or 6. Are they equally likely to move?
Zoe says 6 is the most difficult number to roll. Is she right?
options: Yes, 6 is less likely than the others
No, every number is equally likely

items.q: In a raffle with numbers 1 to 100, how likely is number 1 to be picked compared with number 53?

items: A set of possible outcomes for a trial can be stated by writing a sample space.
Outcomes can be evaluated to decide how likely they are to happen.
By considering the likelihood of outcomes, we can identify when outcomes are equally likely to happen.

blocks.text: Equally likely means the same chance. Check the amount of space, or the number of dice faces, for each outcome.

flashcards.back:
A single predefined test.

Example: spinning a spinner once.

All the possible outcomes of a trial.

Example: ξ = ❴win, lose❵
The chance that a particular event will occur.

flashcards.front: What is the name of the Greek letter ξ, used for a sample space?
flashcards.back:
xi.

It stands for the set of all possible outcomes of a trial.

flashcards.front: A spinner has four equal sectors: two win and two lose. How many outcomes are in its sample space?
flashcards.back:
2.

ξ = ❴win, lose❵. The sample space lists each different outcome once.

flashcards.front: What is the sample space for rolling a regular six-sided dice once?
Ana, Ben and Cal play a board game and the trial is the whole game. What is the sample space?
flashcards.back:
ξ = ❴Ana, Ben, Cal❵

When the trial is a game, the outcomes are the possible winners.

flashcards.front: Two outcomes are equally likely when...
flashcards.back:
They have the same chance (likelihood) of happening.

Example: two equal-sized sectors, win and lose.

flashcards.front: A regular dice is rolled. Is ❴odd, even❵ equally likely?
flashcards.back:
Yes.

There are 3 odd numbers (1, 3, 5) and 3 even numbers (2, 4, 6).

flashcards.front: A regular dice is rolled. Is ❴multiple of 3, not a multiple of 3❵ equally likely?
flashcards.back:
No.

Multiples of 3: 3 and 6 (2 numbers). Not multiples of 3: 1, 2, 4 and 5 (4 numbers).

flashcards.front: A fair coin has not landed on tails for a while. Is tails now more likely?
flashcards.back:
No.

Heads and tails are always equally likely and are not affected by previous results.

flashcards.front: In a raffle with numbers 1 to 100, is number 1 less likely to be picked than number 53?
flashcards.back:
No.

Each number is equally likely to be picked, regardless of its size.

worksheet.title: Worksheet: Equally likely outcomes
worksheet.instructions: Answer each question with a number, a word or a short phrase. Think about the sample space and count the outcomes carefully.

questions.prompt: A trial is one spin of a spinner with four sectors labelled win, lose, win, lose. How many different outcomes are in the sample space?
questions.explanation: The only possible outcomes are win and lose; the sample space lists each different outcome once.

questions.prompt: How many outcomes are in the sample space for rolling a regular six-sided dice once?
questions.explanation: The possible outcomes are the numbers 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 and 6.

questions.prompt: Fill in the gap: a ______ is a single predefined test.
questions.explanation: A trial is a single predefined test, such as spinning a spinner once.

questions.prompt: What name is given to the set of all the possible outcomes of a trial?
questions.explanation: A sample space is all the possible outcomes of a trial.

questions.prompt: A spinner has the sample space ξ = ❴A, B, C, D❵. What is the smallest number of sectors it could have?
questions.explanation: Each of the four letters must appear on at least one sector.

questions.prompt: Alex and Sofia roll a regular six-sided dice. Sofia gets the cookie if the dice shows a multiple of 3. How many numbers on the dice give Sofia the cookie?
questions.explanation: The multiples of 3 on a regular dice are 3 and 6.

questions.prompt: Lucas gets the cookie if a regular dice shows an even number and Jun gets it if it shows an odd number. Are the outcomes equally likely? (yes or no)
questions.explanation: There are 3 even numbers and 3 odd numbers, so each has the same chance.

questions.prompt: In a raffle the tickets are numbered 1 to 100 and one is picked randomly. Is ticket 1 more likely, less likely or equally likely to be picked than ticket 53?
questions.explanation: Each number is equally likely to be picked, regardless of its size.

questions.prompt: Ana, Ben and Cal play a board game. The trial is the whole game and the outcomes are the possible winners. How many outcomes are in the sample space?
questions.explanation: The outcomes are Ana wins, Ben wins and Cal wins.

questions.prompt: A regular dice is rolled. Team A wins on a 1 or 2, Team B wins on a 3, and Team C wins on a 4, 5 or 6. Which team is most likely to win?
questions.explanation: Team C has 3 winning numbers, more than Team A (2) or Team B (1).

questions.prompt: What is the name of the Greek letter ξ that is used to represent a sample space?
questions.explanation: ξ (xi) represents the set of all possible outcomes of a trial.
